Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

ZE1KEgsm_80.description:
Uber just shipped an AI agent that builds your whole grocery cart from a photo of a handwritten list — and the interesting part for builders is how little the LLM actually does.

Their real architecture is a multi-prompt state graph, and most of the boxes are plain deterministic code. The LLM only handles the fuzzy stuff: reading what you meant, judging which product fits. Everything that has to be correct — prices, arithmetic, availability, the cart total — is code the model never touches.

→ The planner LLM doesn't "go shopping" — it emits a structured CartPlan (item, search_terms, item_context, price constraints), then hands it to code
→ "12 eggs" resolves to one carton of twelve via a deterministic quantity step, not free LLM arithmetic
→ A deterministic guardrail can veto a bad output and fall back before it ever reaches your cart
→ The lesson: when an agent is unreliable, the fix usually isn't a bigger model — it's taking responsibility away from the model and moving anything exact into code

The rule to steal: LLM handles meaning, code handles truth.

GRuioEQxe40.description:
A group of AI researchers just published a 90-page plan for what should happen if AI becomes smarter than every human on earth.
The team includes former OpenAI researchers. They did conversations with frontier AI lab employees, policymakers, national security experts, and wrote AI 2040: Plan A.
The proposal is simple to explain and incredibly difficult to pull off.
Get the US and China to agree to delay the development of superintelligence until 2040. Make almost all frontier AI research public. Let dozens of companies catch up instead of allowing a handful of labs to race ahead. And enforce all of it.
The timeline they have is wild.
By 2028, AI companies are pushing to automate fields like law the way they pushed into coding a few years earlier. By 2029, the US and China negotiate a deal. By 2030, AI research has become fully automated, but the agreement slows the race before an intelligence explosion happens.
It's one of the most interesting pieces of AI policy writing I've read this year.

-IrWlbs3FGI.description:
We didn't have footage, but the images of the crash on the Moon have finally arrived, the upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that struck the lunar surface, exactly as predicted in our earlier update.

South Korea's Danuri orbiter, operated by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, captured before-and-after images of the exact impact site, observing the location for about 30 minutes before the collision and another 30 minutes right after, eight observations total. The after-images clearly show a brand new crater that wasn't there before.

Independently, the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile detected two distinct elements in the impact plume, sodium and lithium, each reflecting sunlight differently enough to be told apart. The lithium came from the rocket itself. The sodium came from the Moon's own surface, blasted out on impact.

Two completely independent confirmations, images and chemistry, of the exact same event.

The stage hit at 8,700 kilometres per hour. NASA's latest estimate puts the new crater at roughly 18 metres wide and nearly 4 metres deep. For scale, a natural meteoroid carrying the same energy hits the Moon about once every six days, this wasn't a rare event, we simply knew exactly when and where this one was coming.

NASA and ESA are both still processing their own data, with more observations expected soon.

Source: Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI), Danuri Mission. European Southern Observatory, Very Large Telescope Observations. NASA, Falcon 9 Upper Stage Lunar Impact Analysis.
#MoonImpact #SpaceX #Falcon9 #Danuri #NASA

72zrUOzf1C8.description:
Our solar system briefly had ten planets, and almost nobody remembers the tenth one.

For a short window, the official list read Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto, and Eris. Eris is a trans-Neptunian object with an unusually eccentric orbit, ranging from about 37.9 AU at its closest to roughly 97.5 AU at its farthest from the sun, more than double Pluto's average distance. At its most distant point, temperatures drop low enough that Eris's thin atmosphere condenses and freezes onto its surface as a layer of snow, then thaws again as it swings back closer to the sun.

Before Eris was confirmed in 2005, astronomers had a working assumption, icy trans-Neptunian objects were reliably smaller than Pluto. Eris broke that assumption. It turned out to be roughly 27 percent more massive than Pluto, despite having a slightly smaller diameter, making it denser overall. It also has its own moon, Dysnomia, discovered later that same year.

Eris is named after the Greek goddess of strife and discord, a fitting choice, since its discovery caused exactly that within the astronomical community. The existence of an object rivaling Pluto in mass forced the International Astronomical Union to formally define what a planet actually is for the first time. Under the new 2006 definition, Pluto no longer qualified. Today, both Eris and Pluto are officially classified as dwarf planets.

Source: NASA, Eris Overview. International Astronomical Union, 2006 Planet Definition Resolution. California Institute of Technology, Discovery of Eris (Brown, Trujillo, Rabinowitz).

vFyvzJLcCR8.description:
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Pluto, and it didn't even land, it flew past.

It took NASA's New Horizons probe nine years to reach Pluto after launching in 2006, arriving in July 2015. Before that, the best imagery we had came from the Hubble Space Telescope, low-resolution and unable to resolve any real surface detail. New Horizons changed that entirely, revealing a surface far more geologically complex than anyone expected.

Among the discoveries: Sputnik Planitia, a heart-shaped nitrogen ice glacier roughly a million square miles wide and up to 2.5 miles thick, possible cryovolcanoes, water-ice mountain ranges, canyon systems hundreds of miles long and over two miles deep, and evidence pointing to a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath the icy crust.

Pluto's atmosphere is so thin it barely qualifies as one, and surface temperatures drop to around minus 229 degrees Celsius. Pluto has five known moons, the largest of which, Charon, is over 1,200 kilometres across, more than half Pluto's own diameter and larger than the dwarf planet Ceres. Charon is massive enough that it and Pluto don't orbit each other in the traditional sense, both bodies orbit a shared centre of gravity, or barycenter, that sits outside Pluto's surface. The two are also mutually tidally locked, permanently facing each other.

Pluto's orbit is tilted about 17 degrees relative to the plane the rest of the planets follow, and it's also highly eccentric, between 1979 and 1999, Pluto was actually closer to the Sun than Neptune was. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet, specifically because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, the combined mass of other Kuiper Belt objects sharing its zone outweighs Pluto by roughly 14 times.

Pluto was named in 1930 by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl from Oxford, England.

Source: NASA, New Horizons Mission Overview. NASA, Pluto Facts. International Astronomical Union, 2006 Resolution B5.

BYEeWlHoExE.description:
Google's new robot unscrews a lightbulb nine times out of ten and loses to a trash bag more than half the time, and that one gap tells you which jobs get automated first.

Google DeepMind shipped Gemini Robotics 2 on July 30, and unlike most robot announcements it published the failure rates instead of only the highlight reel. Read those numbers side by side and a very clean line appears. It is not strength and it is not intelligence. The only thing that decides whether a task is basically solved or still years away is whether the object keeps its shape when you touch it, and whether it stays where you left it. Two yeses and the robot is already good at it. One no and it falls off a cliff.

→ Unscrew a lightbulb 92%, precise part insertion 89.6%, pick something off a shelf 76.3% — all rigid, all holding still
→ Tie a trash bag 44%, seal a ziplock 40%, sweep with a dustpan 32% — all soft, all changing shape as the hand closes
→ Same object, different place: off a shelf 76.3%, off the floor 45.7% — the floor hides where the thing actually is
→ Yes, the demo really did tie a knot in a bag, and DeepMind is the one who reported that it works 44 times out of 100
→ So sorting rigid parts, machine tending and packing kits are the jobs that go first
→ And laundry, food prep, bin bags and cable runs are the ones that are still years out

Comment "FLOPPY" and I'll send you the docs link.
Which job in your life is actually floppy?

Everyone talks about better prompts = better AI outputs.

But if you're building AI apps or using LLMs seriously, there's a much bigger question:

How do you know if the AI's answer is actually good?

In this video, we break down 6 essential LLM evaluation metrics:

1. Correctness — Is the answer actually accurate?

2. Groundedness — Is the AI using the information provided, or inventing facts?

3. Relevance — Did the AI actually answer the question?

4. Completeness — Did it cover every important part of the request?

5. Conciseness — Is the response clear and to the point, without unnecessary information?

6. Safety — Is the AI avoiding harmful or dangerous outputs?

These metrics become especially important when you're building AI applications, RAG systems, AI agents, chatbots, or production LLM workflows.

Because prompting an AI is only half the problem.

The other half is knowing whether the output deserves to be trusted.

Xnj5ta_JxLE.description:
Landing on Mars isn't science fiction anymore, it's something we've done repeatedly with robotic missions since 1976, though no human has made the trip yet.

Scientists believe Mars once closely resembled early Earth. Orbital and rover imagery has revealed ancient river channels, dried lakebeds, and geological evidence consistent with a past ocean covering parts of the northern hemisphere. Over billions of years, Mars lost most of its atmosphere and surface water, leaving behind the dry, iron-oxide-covered world we see today, the source of its distinctive red colour.

Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the solar system, standing approximately 21.9 kilometres tall, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest, with a base roughly the size of Arizona. Nearby lies Valles Marineris, a canyon system stretching over 4,000 kilometres in length and reaching depths of up to 7 kilometres, more than ten times longer and several times deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon.

Average surface temperature sits around minus 63 degrees Celsius, dropping to as low as minus 140 at the poles during winter.

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both thought to be captured asteroids. Phobos is gradually spiraling inward due to tidal forces and is expected to either collide with Mars or break apart into a ring system within the next 30 to 50 million years.

One of the most actively studied Martian mysteries involves methane detected by NASA's Curiosity rover, which fluctuates seasonally in ways not yet fully explained. Researchers have not determined whether the source is geological activity or, potentially, biological processes, making it a key focus in the ongoing search for evidence of life.

A Martian day, called a sol, lasts approximately 24 hours and 37 minutes, remarkably close to an Earth day.

Source: NASA, Mars Facts and Exploration. NASA Curiosity Rover, Methane Detection Studies. Wikipedia, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

TRAPPIST-1 is a red dwarf star system located about 40 light-years from Earth in the constellation Aquarius. The star itself is only slightly larger than Jupiter, and because it's so small and dim, its seven confirmed planets all orbit closer to it than Mercury orbits our Sun, meaning the entire seven-planet system would fit comfortably inside Mercury's orbital path. All seven planets are approximately Earth-sized, and at least three, TRAPPIST-1e, f, and g, sit within the star's habitable zone.
TRAPPIST-1e stands out as one of the most promising candidates discovered so far. It is remarkably close to Earth in mass (about 77%), radius (about 91%), density (about 102%), and surface gravity (about 93%), giving it an Earth Similarity Index of 0.95, among the highest ever recorded for a known exoplanet. Scientists believe it may have a compact atmosphere and liquid water oceans, though this remains under active investigation, recent James Webb Space Telescope observations of the system's innermost planets, TRAPPIST-1b and c, found no detectable atmosphere at all, underscoring how much is still unknown about the outer planets like e.
The TRAPPIST-1 system itself is estimated to be around 7.6 billion years old, roughly 3 billion years older than our own solar system, meaning if life exists there, it would have had significantly more time to evolve than life on Earth has.
NASA's Exoplanet Travel Bureau has released a free downloadable poster imagining the view from the surface of TRAPPIST-1e, showing its six sister planets, some appearing far larger in the sky than our own Moon does from Earth. JWST has already dedicated more than 200 hours of observing time specifically to understanding the habitability of this system.
Source: NASA Exoplanet Exploration, TRAPPIST-1 System Overview. NASA Exoplanet Travel Bureau. James Webb Space Telescope, TRAPPIST-1 Observation Program.

What happens when AI stops being just a tool and becomes the team that designs, builds, tests, secures, documents, deploys, and even maintains your software?In this episode of the M365 FM Podcast, Mirko Peters speaks with Mark Smith [MVP], widely known as NZ365Guy, about the transition from traditional Microsoft development toward AI-first software engineering. Mark brings decades of experience across Microsoft technologies, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, Copilot, AI platforms, consulting, training, podcasting, and software development.The conversation goes far beyond Microsoft Copilot. Mark explains how he is building his own AI software factory with specialized autonomous agents, why he uses OpenCLAW as an AI harness, how multiple AI models can work together, why context engineering is becoming more important than basic prompt engineering, and what developers and IT professionals should learn to prepare for the Intelligence Age.

FROM MICROSOFT TRAINING TO THE AI ERA
Mark's journey into the Microsoft ecosystem started around 30 years ago. What began with an interest in learning web design eventually led him into IT training, Microsoft infrastructure, networking, management, Dynamics CRM, Power Platform, Copilot, and AI.He recalls the early days of the web, when technologies such as HTML and CSS were still relatively new to many organizations and Microsoft NT4 was becoming increasingly important. Over seven years, Mark progressed from selling technical training to delivering courses himself and eventually becoming general manager of the company.That experience created the foundation for a career that would continuously evolve alongside Microsoft's technology stack.

FROM DYNAMICS CRM TO POWER PLATFORM AND AI
Mark describes how his Microsoft journey moved from early Microsoft CRM into Dynamics 365 and later Power Platform. He was attracted to CRM not simply as a sales system, but as a platform that could be used to create many different kinds of business applications.Power Platform continued that evolution through low-code development. But Mark believes the next transition is significantly larger.AI is changing the interface between humans and software development itself. Instead of spending hours navigating configuration screens and traditional user interfaces, developers increasingly have the ability to communicate their desired outcomes through prompts, APIs, MCP interfaces, command-line tools, and AI agents.For Mark, this represents a fundamental shift away from traditional low-code development toward AI-first software creation.

THE MOMENT GENERATIVE AI CHANGED EVERYTHING
Mark began exploring AI years before ChatGPT, particularly around machine learning and Microsoft's Cognitive Services. However, the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022 made the scale of the coming transformation much clearer.Another important moment came when he experimented with early Copilot capabilities inside Power Platform. During a Microsoft MVP session, he was able to prompt an application into existence while the technology was being demonstrated.That experience reinforced an idea that would increasingly shape his work: software creation was becoming conversational.

WHY MARK EXPANDED BEYOND THE MICROSOFT AI ECOSYSTEM
Although Mark has spent decades working with Microsoft technology, his current AI environment is deliberately multi-model.He discusses his experience with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft models, Chinese AI models, European models, and other providers. Rather than designing systems around one vendor, he wants the ability to select the best model for a particular task.This approach reduces dependency on any single AI provider and allows the underlying models to change without rebuilding the entire system.The model becomes a replaceable component rather than the center of the architecture.

TRUST, DATA SOVEREIGNTY AND MICROSOFT AI
The discussion also explores why Microsoft's ecosystem remains important for enterprise AI.For regulated organizations, the location where AI inference happens can matter significantly. Data sovereignty, compliance requirements, infrastructure location, and third-party model providers can all affect whether an AI architecture is acceptable.Mark explains that he is developing software where Microsoft's own models and infrastructure can provide an important trust advantage. Organizations that already trust Microsoft's cloud environment may prefer AI workloads that remain within that ecosystem.This becomes particularly important in countries and industries where data cannot easily leave a specific jurisdiction.

WHAT IS AN AI SOFTWARE FACTORY?
One of the central topics of the episode is Mark's concept of an AI software factory.Traditionally, software projects require multiple specialized roles: requirements analysts, architects, developers, engineering managers, testers, security specialists, documentation teams, and release managers.Mark asked a different question:What happens if each of thos...

In this episode, Tremain Davis sits down with Joe Paul, Founder and CEO of Optima Nova AI, for a conversation about making artificial intelligence accessible to everyone, especially communities and organizations that have historically been left behind by technological change.

Joe shares why he believes AI can democratize opportunity for nonprofits, small and medium-sized businesses, solopreneurs, and underserved communities. They explore the growing digital divide, the importance of AI literacy, and why access alone isn’t enough—we also need to teach people how to actually use the technology.

The conversation also gets practical. Connor Leahy has spent his career at the frontier of AI, from reverse-engineering GPT-2 as a student and co-founding EleutherAI to building the AI safety company Conjecture. He now leads US policy work at ControlAI, and he returns to the show with a warning that has stopped being theoretical: AI systems are escaping their sandboxes, writing their own zero-days and leaving each other notes on how to break out.

Peter and Connor discuss the OpenAI incident that ended in an attack on Hugging Face sophisticated enough to be mistaken for a state actor, why we understand almost nothing about how these systems work, how reinforcement learning produces models that lie, cheat and manipulate to reach a goal and why the next stage after chatbots and agents is swarms.

But Connor’s argument is that the future is not decided. He believes superintelligence should be treated the way nuclear weapons are treated, banned and verified and deterred and that the real bottleneck is awareness rather than opposition. They discuss what an “aligned” superintelligence would actually mean, why military people understand the threat faster than technologists and what ordinary people can do about it.

MltAATjd_BQ.description:
China Just Bypassed CUDA — Jensen Huang’s "Horrible Outcome" Just Happened

For two decades, Nvidia's CUDA software platform was the invisible foundation of the entire global AI industry. Not the hardware — the software. A proprietary ecosystem so deeply embedded into research labs, cloud providers, and AI frameworks that AMD and Intel spent billions trying to crack it and failed.

Then the United States government tried to use it as a weapon.

In 2022, Washington began restricting Nvidia's most advanced AI chips from reaching China. The strategy was logical: cut off the hardware, stall the AI development. What followed was the opposite of the intended outcome.

Denied access to American silicon, Chinese engineers had no choice but to go deeper into the machine than anyone expected. DeepSeek's engineers bypassed CUDA entirely, dropping down to PTX — Nvidia's own low-level instruction set — and used the open-source Triton compiler to hand-optimize training runs on legally restricted hardware. The results matched the world's frontier models.

Huawei responded by building the CloudMatrix 384 — a rack-scale supernode linking 384 Ascend 910C processors through a full optical mesh, delivering approximately 300 petaFLOPs of dense compute, exceeding Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 in raw throughput. Then Huawei open-sourced its entire CANN software toolkit, directly attacking the developer lock-in that had protected Nvidia's moat for twenty years.

Nvidia took a $4.5 billion write-down on its China-compliant H20 chip. China's regulators formally instructed domestic tech giants to stop buying American chips altogether. Jensen Huang publicly confirmed his company's advanced AI chip market share in China had collapsed from approximately 95% to zero.

This documentary investigates the full technical and geopolitical story — the BIS export control thresholds that triggered the crisis, the PTX-level engineering that cracked the software moat, the CloudMatrix optical interconnect strategy, and what a permanently bifurcated global AI ecosystem means for the rest of the world.

In this podcast, Algo Sid breaks down how a trading strategy can be taken from a simple idea on YouTube and converted into a fully automated trading system. The conversation begins with an important question: is algo trading actually profitable? He explains why looking only at returns can be misleading and why traders need to consider the complete performance picture, including drawdown, number of trades, slippage, brokerage and other trading costs.

The discussion then moves to the growing use of AI in trading, including an AI trading leaderboard where different models are given capital and allowed to trade. This leads to an important lesson about why a strategy showing 100% or 150% returns on paper does not automatically make it a good strategy. Algo Sid explains how high trading frequency, large drawdowns and execution costs can significantly change the real performance of a strategy.

The main part of the podcast focuses on a practical challenge: taking the Hilega Milega strategy and automating it from scratch. Starting with the strategy rules, he explains how to convert the logic into code, create buy and sell signals, use TradingView alerts, and connect those signals to a backend. He also explains the difference between backtesting, forward testing, paper trading and live automation, and why each stage matters before putting real money at risk.

The final section takes the process one step further by showing how automated orders can be placed using Python, alerts and broker APIs. He explains how a signal can travel from the indicator to the backend and eventually trigger an order through the broker, along with some of the practical issues that can arise during automation. If you want to understand algo trading, AI in trading, strategy automation, TradingView alerts, Python, APIs, backtesting, forward testing and automated order placement, this episode gives you a practical look at how the entire process works from start to finish.

4ZfJYAnbH8w.description:
Are you tired of AI assistants generating broken code, insecure implementations, database-killing N+1 queries, or hallucinated API calls that fail in production?

In this video, we explore how to move beyond basic prompting and build a structured, production-grade software development workflow with AI.

We walk through the complete Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) and how tools like Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Windsurf can be used effectively across planning, architecture, implementation, testing, security, code review, CI/CD, and monitoring.

The Golden Rule

Architecture first. AI generation second.

AI is extremely good at implementing established patterns, but it is much less reliable at deciding which patterns and architectural boundaries are appropriate for your specific system.

The goal isn’t to let AI build everything for you. The goal is to design the right boundaries first and then use AI to accelerate development without sacrificing quality, security, or maintainability.

What You’ll Learn

* Planning and architecture with AI
* Creating effective project documentation such as ARCHITECTURE.md and DECISIONS.md
* Rules for building AI-friendly codebases
* Writing explicit, maintainable code
* Dependency injection and clear architectural boundaries
* Working in small, verifiable implementation units
* Using AI for test and edge-case generation
* Security review of AI-generated code
* Preventing SQL injection, SSRF, secret exposure, and over-permissive authorization
* CI/CD strategies for AI-generated code
* Feature flags and automated rollbacks
* Structured logging and production monitoring
* The importance of human judgment and code review

The Core Idea

Don’t ask AI:

“Build my application.”

Instead, give it a well-defined architecture, constraints, conventions, interfaces, tests, and acceptance criteria — then let AI help you implement and validate each small piece.

AI should accelerate engineering judgment, not replace it.
